analysis.one_liner: Bans firing, refusing to hire, or mistreating workers because they are gay, lesbian, or bisexual.
analysis.headline: The Senate defeated the bill 49-50 on September 10, 1996, one vote short of passage, with 41 of 47 Democrats in favor and only 8 of 53 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for employers with 15 or more workers to discriminate against employees because of their sexual orientation, whether real or perceived. It covered private employers, federal agencies, and congressional employees, and enforced the ban through the same Equal Employment Opportunity Commission process used for race and sex discrimination. The Senate debated it for a few days and voted it down by a single vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers (including people believed to be gay) at covered employers would gain a federal right to sue over hiring, firing, promotion, and pay discrimination, with remedies and attorney's fees modeled on existing civil rights law.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered employers from treating workers differently, or discriminating based on who they are believed to associate with, because of sexual orientation, defined to include orientations that are 'real or perceived' [S3].
Covers private employers with 15 or more employees as well as federal agencies and congressional workplaces, extending the same protection government employees would get [S3].

Enforces the ban through the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the courts using the same procedures and remedies as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, including possible attorney's fees for prevailing workers [S2] [S3].

Bars states from claiming immunity from federal lawsuits under this Act and makes the United States liable for remedies (except punitive damages), so government employers could be held accountable [S2] [S3].
Prohibits retaliation against workers who file complaints or help investigations, and requires employers to post notices of the new rights [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers with 15 or more employees would bear new compliance duties and exposure to discrimination claims and damages. The federal government would be liable for monetary remedies against itself.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require employers to provide benefits to an employee's partner, so same-sex partners would remain excluded from health and other benefits [S2] [S3].
It excludes the armed forces entirely, so the military's rules at the time (including the ban on gay service members then in force) would be untouched [S3].

Religious organizations are largely exempt, employers with fewer than 15 employees are not covered, and a worker cannot bring a 'disparate impact' claim proving a neutral practice disproportionately excludes gay workers [S2] [S3].

Critics in the Senate argued during debate that the measure would create new litigation exposure for employers and expand federal power over private workplaces; the bill addressed part of this by explicitly prohibiting quotas and preferential treatment [S5] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 15-plus-employee workplaces it covered, the bill offered real legal protection against being fired or refused a job for being gay, at a compliance cost to employers comparable to other civil rights mandates. Its carve-outs — no partner benefits, a broad religious exemption, exclusion of the military and small employers, and no disparate-impact claims — made it a narrow version of the protection it promised.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate took it up within days of introduction and voted it down on the floor, 49 to 50 — one vote short of the majority needed to pass.

narrative.text: Sen. Kennedy introduced the bill on September 5, 1996, and it was immediately placed on the Senate calendar, meaning it was ready for floor action without going through a committee [S5].
The Senate considered the bill on September 6 and again on September 10 [S5].
On September 10, 1996, the Senate rejected the bill on an up-or-down vote, 49-50 (Record Vote No. 281) [S6].
The vote split heavily by party: 41 of 47 Democrats voted yes but only 8 of 53 Republicans did [S6].
Because the bill never passed the Senate, the House never considered it, and the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 without the bill becoming law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and the senators who voted no are better off: no federal sexual orientation discrimination mandate took effect, and workplaces remained governed only by state and local laws where those existed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who opposed the new mandate

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed its Senate floor consideration

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged Congress to pass the employment nondiscrimination bill during the 1996 debate

against.name: 45 of 53 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage, providing the bulk of the votes against the bill

sides.party_line_note: The vote broke largely on party lines: 41 of 47 Democrats voted yes while only 8 of 53 Republicans did, leaving the bill one vote short at 49-50 [S6].

industries.note: The bill would have exposed these employers to discrimination claims, damages, and posting requirements based on sexual orientation. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran directly against the protection workers would have gained.

industries.industry: Federal government and Congress as employers
industries.note: The federal government would have become liable for monetary remedies (except punitive damages) against itself for sexual orientation discrimination, while its own employees would have gained the protection.
The bill carved religious organizations out of the ban (except for their for-profit activities), letting them hire according to their own doctrines.
